problem: VLMs used for robot control (GPT-4o/4V, LLaVA, Qwen-VL, SpatialVLM) express actions in language or bounding boxes. This is too imprecise when a command identifies an object by spatial relation, or points to object-free space ('place the cup next to the plate'). Prior VLM-for-robotics methods (Code-as-Policies, VoxPoser, MOKA, PIVOT) also rely on pre-defined primitives, external object detectors, or iterative visual prompting, and demonstration-based models (RT-1/RT-2/Octo) need costly real-world data.
motivation: Pointing is a natural and precise way to communicate where to act. Image points can be lifted to 3D with depth and read as grasp contacts, placement regions or navigation waypoints. The authors observe that in-context learning cannot teach a VLM a new output format, whereas instruction tuning on cheap, automatically labeled synthetic data can. That synthetic data (procedural 3D scenes with computed spatial relations) scales far better than human demonstrations.
key_idea: Instruction-tune a LLaVA-style VLM to output lists of normalized 2D image points ('spatial affordances') satisfying relational language instructions. Training uses a procedurally generated synthetic dataset of object-reference and free-space-reference points, co-trained with real VQA and LVIS detection data.
insight: Precise, relation-aware pointing is mostly a data problem, not an architecture problem. A plain LLaVA-1.5-13B tuned on templated synthetic data transfers to real images and natural language: 49.82% on RoboRefIt and 46.77% on Where2Place, vs ≤29.06% for GPT-4o with bbox visual prompting. It keeps VQA performance on par with LLaVA-1.5-13B. The data-mix ablation on Where2Place shows which sources matter: removing free-space reference data collapses accuracy (46.77→13.21), removing real VQA data costs 18 points (→28.28), removing LVIS gives 34.27, removing object reference gives 42.23, and using only 10% of the data gives 15.71. So synthetic free-space labels, real-image co-training and data scale all matter. In-context examples do not substitute for tuning: GPT-4o-ICL (9.01) is worse than zero-shot GPT-4o (15.28) on RoboRefIt, and ICL gives zero accuracy for Qwen-VL and LLaVA-NeXT. A design trick helps too: colored bounding-box visual prompts mark reference objects in the synthetic images at train time only, so the synthetic data teaches relational reasoning while grounding comes from LVIS.
method: Spatial affordance formulation: output a set of normalized (x,y) image coordinates satisfying the instruction's relation, instead of language actions or bounding boxes. At deployment, points are lifted to 3D with a depth map and sent to a motion planner (manipulation, with an end-effector offset) or a simple path planner (navigation).

Model/instruction tuning: LLaVA-1.5 recipe with a CLIP ViT-L/14-336px encoder (frozen), a 2-layer MLP projector (pretrained on LAION-CC-SBU 558K) and Vicuna-v1.5-13B. The projector and LLM are fine-tuned with an autoregressive response-token loss; 40 h on 16 A100s, batch 16/GPU, lr 4e-5.

Procedural synthetic scene generation: randomized kitchen-like layouts with articulated furniture (revolute/prismatic joints) and ACRONYM objects (8K+ instances, 262 categories) placed in stable, collision-free poses on support surfaces. Random cameras are kept only if they see ≥3 visible objects and ≥1 valid relation; ~660K (image, relation) pairs come from 10K scenes.

Relation and label computation: 3D bounding boxes give pairwise relations (left, right, in front, behind, above, below, next to, on, inside, on left/right/front/back part). Object-reference labels are 1–50 points sampled in the target object's mask.

Free-space affordance generation: compute the relation for a target object, remove the object, re-render, and sample points in the intersection of the removed object's footprint with its supporting surface. This gives labels for vacant regions that have no visual cue.

Train-only visual prompts plus data co-training: reference objects are marked with colored rectangles in the synthetic images (not at test time). Training mixes 347K object-reference, 320K free-space-reference, 665K LLaVA-v1.5 VQA and 100K LVIS bbox examples in one unified format, which preserves general VQA ability and teaches grounding.

setting.backbone: LLaVA-1.5-style VLM: CLIP ViT-L/14-336px (frozen) + 2-layer MLP projector + Vicuna-v1.5-13B (projector and LLM fine-tuned)
setting.training_data: ~667K synthetic points data (347K object reference + 320K free-space reference; ~660K image-relation pairs from 10K procedurally generated scenes with ACRONYM objects) + 665K LLaVA-v1.5 VQA conversations + 100K LVIS detection examples converted to bbox-center/size text; no real robot data or demonstrations
setting.observation: single RGB image + language instruction (depth map used only to lift predicted 2D points to 3D)
setting.action_space: 2D image keypoints (normalized coordinates) projected to 3D targets; executed by a motion planner (manipulation) or a simple path planner (navigation)
setting.simulator: custom procedural photorealistic scene generator for training data; CoppeliaSim (YouBot) for navigation eval; real world for manipulation and AR
setting.privileged: none for prediction. Depth is used for 2D→3D projection, and execution relies on an external motion/path planner (map/planner details not specified for CoppeliaSim).

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark is evaluated. Navigation is only a small custom CoppeliaSim study, reported as per-task success counts (x/5) in a figure-embedded table. The free-space benchmark name is a LaTeX macro in the source; it is resolved here as Where2Place, the name used in the published paper. RoboRefIt evaluation uses a 750-image subset whose source split is not stated. The abstract's '21.8%' (affordance accuracy) and '30.5%' (downstream success) gains over GPT-4o/PIVOT are aggregate claims without a detailed breakdown. The VQA benchmark numbers are grouped into one entry.
results: RoboPoint reaches 49.82% on RoboRefIt, 46.77% on Where2Place and 44.48% on Where2Place's unseen-relation subset. This beats all VLM baselines, including GPT-4o (15.28 / 29.06 / 27.14), Qwen-VL (24.08 on RoboRefIt), LLaVA-NeXT-34B and SpaceLLaVA, and it matches LLaVA-1.5-13B on eight VQA benchmarks. In real-world manipulation (7 tasks × 10 trials) it beats GPT-4V, the best baseline, by 39.5% average success; PIVOT and Qwen-VL score lower. In CoppeliaSim navigation it reaches 5/5 on five tasks where GPT-4V scores 0/5 on all tasks. It loses to PIVOT on the two 'between furniture' tasks (1/5 vs 3/5 and 2/5), so it wins in 2 of 3 scenes.
limitations: No confidence estimates for predicted points, and the number of output points is not controllable (stated by the authors).

Navigation evidence is thin: 3 hand-made CoppeliaSim rooms with 5 trials per task. Single-view goal-point prediction only, with no memory, exploration or multi-step planning, and it underperforms PIVOT on the 'between fridge/oven/drawer' tasks.

Synthetic data uses templated language and kitchen-style tabletop/furniture scenes with a fixed relation set. Evaluation sets are small (100 Where2Place images, 750-image RoboRefIt subset, 10 real trials per task).
